input:
In this worked example, we will calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction from its rate constant, together with the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min. The calculation gives a half-life of 15.1 min and a fraction remaining of 0.06.
The rate constant k = 0.046 min-1 was measured at 323 K, from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min, a record which covers several half-lives and therefore fixes the constant from the shape of the decay rather than from any single reading. For a first-order reaction, the half-life t1/2 is fixed by the rate constant through the relation t1/2 = ln(2) / k, where k denotes the rate constant and t1/2 is the time in which the concentration falls to half its starting value. It is worth noting that the half-life so defined contains no concentration: the time a sample takes to halve is the same wherever the decay is started, and this independence of the starting concentration is the hallmark of the first-order law. Substituting the measured value gives t1/2 = ln(2) / 0.046 = 15.1 min. Furthermore, the fraction remaining after a time t is given by exp(-k t), a relation that carries no half-life in it and applies at any time. The fraction relation and the half-life relation are essentially the same law in two forms: setting t at one half-life in the exponential returns exactly the halving that the first relation states. At 60 min, substitution gives exp(-0.046 x 60) = 0.06. Reassuringly, the two results agree with each other: 60 min is close to four half-lives of 15.1 min, and a quantity that halves four times is naturally left small; the computed fraction of 0.06 is of exactly that size. At the other end of the range, a time short against the half-life leaves a fraction close to the starting amount, and the exponential gives that as well, so the relation behaves correctly at both ends. It is important to remember, however, that both relations hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither the half-life relation nor the exponential fraction applies to it.
